title: The moment of the action
titleJp: 食べるところ・食べているところ・食べたところ
canDo: I can say which moment of an action I'm at: about to start (出かけるところ), right in the middle (作っているところ) or just after (着いたところ).
I can explain why I can't take a call right now: 今、晩ご飯を作っているところだから、あとでかけ直すね。
I can say that something happened only a short while ago, from my point of view, with 〜たばかり — also before a noun (買ったばかりのスマホ).
I can choose between 〜たところ and 〜たばかり depending on how much time has passed and what the sentence is for.
I can recognize 〜るところだった ("almost…") and the 〜たところ、 of news reports ("when X was done, …").

blocks.t: Warm-up: say aloud the dictionary, ている and た forms of 出かける, 着く, 浴びる, 始める and 食べる
Vocabulary: tap 🔊 on each word and repeat it twice; save the words you don't know yet with Mining (⛏), each inside one sentence from this lesson, so they enter your SRS
Grammar: the 2 points, with the examples read aloud and one 🔬 each; in point b, take your time with the たところ × たばかり contrast
Video and reading from block 6, pausing on the examples
Notebook homework + checking it against the answer key
Checklist (block 10) + write your questions in the lesson notebook

skills: The dictionary, ている and た forms of any verb, without hesitating (lessons 07-1, 08-1 and 09-1). In this lesson, that form alone is what changes the meaning of ところ.
〜ので and 〜のに (lessons 12-2 and 22-2), which often appear together with たばかり.
〜てしまう / 〜ちゃう (lesson 18-2), which appears in some examples.
Reading N4 kanji, even slowly. Every sentence comes with its full reading in kana.

vocab.en: place; in this lesson: the point (the moment) of an action
after the た form: only a short while ago…
exactly; ちょうど今 = right now, this very moment
to go out (leave home to go somewhere)
to get used to (〜に慣れる)
to crack, to break (glass, a screen)

grammar.title: 〜るところ / 〜ているところ / 〜たところ
grammar.gloss: about to · right in the middle of · have just
grammar.explanation:
ところ means "place", but it also names places you can't touch — a **point in time**, a stage in the progress of something. English does the same with "point" ("at this point", "the point where…"). Here ところ marks which moment of the action you are at. English needs three different phrases for this ("about to", "in the middle of", "just"); Japanese uses one word, ところ, and lets the **verb form before ところ** choose the moment. ところ is a noun, so the verb phrase in front of it simply describes it (lesson 09-2): 出かけるところ = "the point of going out".
• **Dictionary form + ところ** = about to. The action hasn't started yet, but it's starting now: 今から出かけるところです (I'm just about to go out; I'm still at home).
• **ている + ところ** = right in the middle. The action is happening at this moment: 今、晩ご飯を作っているところです.
• **た + ところ** = have just. The action finished moments ago: ちょうど今、着いたところです.

In the sentence, [verb + ところ] + です／だ is the **PREDICATE**. Read from the end: ところです says "it's the moment of…", and the verb form says which moment. In casual speech the だ usually drops: 今、出るところ！
• Words that often come along: 今から／これから (るところ), 今 (ているところ), ちょうど今 (たところ).
• Why not just say 作っています? That's also correct, but ているところ **puts the focus on the moment**. That's why it is so common for explaining why you can't do something else right now: 今、作っているところだから、あとでかけ直すね。

**Two uses to recognize:**
• **るところだった** = "almost…": もう少しで終電に乗り遅れるところだった (I almost missed the last train). It nearly happened, but it didn't. With ちょうど it can also be "I was just about to…": ちょうど電話するところだった (I was just about to call you).
• **たところ、** with a comma and a continuation, common in news and reports, means "when X was done, (it turned out that) Y": 調べたところ、〜がわかりました. Here it does not mean "have just".
• Going further (Sakubi): ところ can also be a "point" of a person or a thing — a side, a feature: 田中さんの優しいところが好きです ("I like Tanaka's kind side"); この町のいいところは、静かなところです ("the good thing about this town is that it's quiet").
grammar.structure: [dictionary form] ところ (about to) · [ている form] ところ (in the middle) · [た form] ところ (have just) + です／だ

examples.jp: 今から家を出るところです。— じゃあ、駅で待っていますね。
examples.kana: いまからいえをでるところです。— じゃあ、えきでまっていますね。
examples.romaji: Ima kara ie o deru tokoro desu. — Jā, eki de matte imasu ne.
examples.en: I'm just about to leave the house. — OK, then I'll be waiting at the station.

examples.jp: 今、晩ご飯を作っているところだから、あとでかけ直すね。
examples.kana: いま、ばんごはんをつくっているところだから、あとでかけなおすね。
examples.romaji: Ima, bangohan o tsukutte iru tokoro dakara, ato de kakenaosu ne.
examples.en: I'm in the middle of making dinner, so I'll call you back later, OK?

examples.jp: ちょうど今、空港に着いたところです。
examples.kana: ちょうどいま、くうこうについたところです。
examples.romaji: Chōdo ima, kūkō ni tsuita tokoro desu.
examples.en: I've just this moment arrived at the airport.

pitfalls: The form before ところ is what changes the meaning: 食べるところ (I'm about to eat) ≠ 食べているところ (I'm eating right now) ≠ 食べたところ (I've just eaten). Check the form before you translate.
ているところ is only for an action happening right now, never for a state or a habit: 東京に住んでいるところです ✗ → 東京に住んでいます ✓; 毎朝走っているところです ✗ → 毎朝走っています ✓.
たところ means "just now". It doesn't work for a longer stretch of time: 先週引っ越したところです ✗ → 先週引っ越したばかりです ✓ (point b).
Don't mix up るところだった (it almost happened, and didn't) and たところ (it just happened). You made the train, just barely: 乗り遅れたところです ✗ (= I've just missed it) → 乗り遅れるところでした ✓ (= I almost missed it).
howToStudy: In your notebook, draw a timeline with three marks: before · during · after. Under each mark, write the same action with ところ: 食べるところ / 食べているところ / 食べたところ. Repeat with 出かける, 読む and 始める.

🔬 Anatomy → Analyze: paste example 2. 今 shows up as TIME, 晩ご飯を as OBJECT, 作っているところだから as REASON (it ends in から) and かけ直すね as the PREDICATE. Read the predicate first ("I'll call you back") and only then ask: why?
Speaking: imagine a friend calls you three times. Answer out loud, once with each moment: 今から出るところ。／今、シャワーを浴びているところ。／今、駅に着いたところ。

grammar.title: 〜たばかり (and the contrast with 〜たところ)
grammar.gloss: only a short while ago… (as the speaker feels it)
grammar.explanation:
た + ばかり is also translated "have just", but it looks at time in a different way. English uses "just" for both; Japanese splits them by **how you measure the time**. ばかり says **"only a short time ago, as I feel it"**. That short time can be minutes, days or months: 先月日本に来たばかりです (I came last month, and to me that's still recent).
• [verb-た + ばかり] works like a noun: たばかりです／たばかりだ, たばかりなので, たばかりなのに and, before another noun, **たばかりの + N**: 買ったばかりのスマホ (a phone I've just bought), 生まれたばかりの赤ちゃん (a newborn baby).
• A sentence with ばかり often carries a **justification or a surprise**: 始めたばかりなので、まだ下手です (I only just started, so I'm still bad at it); 買ったばかりなのに、もう割れた (I only just bought it, and it's already broken).

**たところ × たばかり**
• **たところ**: the moment **right after**, measured by the clock. It only works for "just now" and often comes with ちょうど今.
• **たばかり**: **a short time, from the speaker's point of view**. It works for just now and also for days or months.
• Quick test: ask "how long ago?". If it was moments ago, both work: 今、起きたところ (I woke up this very moment) / 起きたばかりだから、まだ頭が働かない (I only just woke up, so my brain isn't working yet). If it was days or months ago, only ばかり: 先週引っ越したばかり ✓.
• Before a noun, only ばかりの: 買ったばかりの靴 ✓. ところ can't build "newly X".

Careful: ばかり also means **"only, nothing but"** in other constructions: お菓子ばかり食べる (eats nothing but sweets), 遊んでばかりいる (does nothing but play). What gives the "have just" meaning is the **た form** before ばかり.
• Going further (Sakubi): that "nothing but" ばかり is not the same as だけ ("only"). だけ draws a line: お菓子だけ食べた = I ate only sweets (and nothing else). ばかり fills the whole picture: お菓子ばかり食べている = it's sweets, sweets, sweets — often a complaint about a habit.
grammar.structure: [verb-た] ばかり です／だ · [verb-た] ばかりの [N] · [verb-た] ばかりなので／なのに …

examples.jp: 先月ブラジルから来たばかりなので、まだ日本の生活に慣れていません。
examples.kana: せんげつブラジルからきたばかりなので、まだにほんのせいかつになれていません。
examples.romaji: Sengetsu Burajiru kara kita bakari na node, mada Nihon no seikatsu ni narete imasen.
examples.en: I only came from Brazil last month, so I'm not used to life in Japan yet.

examples.jp: このスマホ、買ったばかりなのに、もう画面が割れちゃった。
examples.kana: このスマホ、かったばかりなのに、もうがめんがわれちゃった。
examples.romaji: Kono sumaho, katta bakari na noni, mō gamen ga warechatta.
examples.en: I only just bought this phone, and the screen has already cracked.

examples.jp: 生まれたばかりの赤ちゃんは、ほとんど一日中寝ています。
examples.kana: うまれたばかりのあかちゃんは、ほとんどいちにちじゅうねています。
examples.romaji: Umareta bakari no akachan wa, hotondo ichinichijū nete imasu.
examples.en: Newborn babies sleep almost all day long. [lit. babies that have just been born]

pitfalls: For a long stretch of time, only ばかり: 三か月前に始めたところです ✗ → 三か月前に始めたばかりです ✓.
"Newly X" before a noun takes の: 買ったばかり靴 ✗ → 買ったばかりの靴 ✓.
食べたばかり (I've just eaten) ≠ 食べてばかり (I do nothing but eat). One kana changes everything: た + ばかり = have just; て + ばかり + いる = do nothing but that. 食べてばかりです ✗ (for "I've just eaten") → 食べたばかりです ✓.
In casual speech you'll hear ばっかり or ばっか: 来たばっかり, 来たばっか. It's the same thing, just more emphatic and informal. In writing and with your boss: 来たばっかりです ✗ → 来たばかりです ✓.
howToStudy: In your notebook, write 3 new things in your life with たばかり + a consequence: 日本語の勉強を始めたばかりなので…／買ったばかりの〜／〜たばかりなのに…
Run the "how long ago?" test on the sentences you wrote. If it was days or months ago, check that you used ばかり and not ところ.

Tap 🔬 on example 1, then cover it and rebuild it from the end, out loud: start with 慣れていません (PREDICATE), then 生活に and 日本の, then まだ, and finally the REASON chunk 来たばかりなので, with ブラジルから and 先月 in front of it.

homework.intro: Do it by hand in your notebook. Write with the kanji you already know and use kana for the rest. Only then open the answer key, item by item. Circle what you got wrong and redo it the next day.

tasks.prompt: Fill in the verb in brackets + ところ, choosing the right form for the moment described in parentheses.

items.q: (You're at the door with your coat on, but you haven't left yet.) 今から＿＿ところです。［出かける］

a.jp: 今から出かけるところです。
a.kana: いまからでかけるところです。

items.note: It hasn't started yet: dictionary form.

items.q: (Your phone rings in the middle of dinner.) 今、ご飯を＿＿ところだから、あとでかけ直すね。［食べる］

a.jp: 今、ご飯を食べているところだから、あとでかけ直すね。
a.kana: いま、ごはんをたべているところだから、あとでかけなおすね。
a.romaji: Ima, gohan o tabete iru tokoro dakara, ato de kakenaosu ne.

items.q: (You've walked in the door this very moment.) ちょうど今、家に＿＿ところです。［帰る］

a.jp: ちょうど今、家に帰ったところです。
a.kana: ちょうどいま、いえにかえったところです。
a.romaji: Chōdo ima, ie ni kaetta tokoro desu.

items.q: (The meeting starts in a minute.) これから会議を＿＿ところです。［始める］

a.jp: これから会議を始めるところです。
a.kana: これからかいぎをはじめるところです。
a.romaji: Kore kara kaigi o hajimeru tokoro desu.

items.q: (A coworker asks if you've read the email yet. You're reading it right now.) 今、＿＿ところです。［読む］

a.jp: 今、読んでいるところです。
a.kana: いま、よんでいるところです。

tasks.prompt: Fill in ところ or ばかり. In one of the items both work: say which one and why.

a.jp: 先週日本に来たばかりです。
a.kana: せんしゅうにほんにきたばかりです。
a.romaji: Senshū Nihon ni kita bakari desu.

items.note: A week is too long for たところ. ばかり shows that, for the speaker, it still feels recent.

items.q: 買った＿＿の靴なのに、もう汚れちゃった。

a.jp: 買ったばかりの靴なのに、もう汚れちゃった。
a.kana: かったばかりのくつなのに、もうよごれちゃった。
a.romaji: Katta bakari no kutsu na noni, mō yogorechatta.

items.note: Before a noun, only ばかりの.

items.q: もしもし、今どこ？— ちょうど今、駅に着いた＿＿。

a.jp: もしもし、今どこ？— ちょうど今、駅に着いたところ。
a.kana: もしもし、いまどこ？— ちょうどいま、えきについたところ。
a.romaji: Moshimoshi, ima doko? — Chōdo ima, eki ni tsuita tokoro.

items.note: Both work. ところ is the most natural for "this very moment" and goes well with ちょうど今, but 着いたばかり is also correct.

items.q: 日本語の勉強を始めた＿＿なので、まだ漢字があまり読めません。

a.jp: 日本語の勉強を始めたばかりなので、まだ漢字があまり読めません。
a.kana: にほんごのべんきょうをはじめたばかりなので、まだかんじがあまりよめません。
a.romaji: Nihongo no benkyō o hajimeta bakari na node, mada kanji ga amari yomemasen.

items.note: A justification based on how recent it feels: ばかり.

items.q: これから晩ご飯を作る＿＿だけど、一緒に食べる？

a.jp: これから晩ご飯を作るところだけど、一緒に食べる？
a.kana: これからばんごはんをつくるところだけど、いっしょにたべる？
a.romaji: Kore kara bangohan o tsukuru tokoro da kedo, issho ni taberu?

items.note: Before starting (dictionary form): only ところ. ばかり needs た before it.

items.q: I've just woken up, this very moment. (use ところ)

a.kana: いま、おきたところです。

items.q: I only moved into this apartment last month.

a.jp: 先月このアパートに引っ越したばかりです。
a.kana: せんげつこのアパートにひっこしたばかりです。
a.romaji: Sengetsu kono apāto ni hikkoshita bakari desu.

items.note: A month ago: only ばかり.

items.q: I'm in the middle of a shower, so I'll call you later, OK? (casual)

a.jp: 今、シャワーを浴びているところだから、あとで電話するね。
a.kana: いま、シャワーをあびているところだから、あとででんわするね。
a.romaji: Ima, shawā o abite iru tokoro dakara, ato de denwa suru ne.

items.q: I almost missed the last train.

a.jp: もう少しで終電に乗り遅れるところだった。
a.kana: もうすこしでしゅうでんにのりおくれるところだった。
a.romaji: Mō sukoshi de shūden ni noriokureru tokoro datta.

items.note: るところだった = it almost happened, but it didn't.

items.q: This is a phone I just bought.

a.jp: これは買ったばかりのスマホです。
a.kana: これはかったばかりのスマホです。
a.romaji: Kore wa katta bakari no sumaho desu.

items.note: "Newly bought" before a noun: ばかりの.

tasks.prompt: Write 4 true sentences: 3 about your day today, one for each moment (るところ, ているところ, たところ), and 1 with たばかり about something new in your life. Read them aloud and record yourself on your phone.

items.q: Model (match its structure, not its words):

a.jp: ちょうど今、晩ご飯を食べたところです。今は、この文を書いているところです。これから日本語の復習をするところです。先月この教科書を買ったばかりなので、まだ少ししか読んでいません。
a.kana: ちょうどいま、ばんごはんをたべたところです。いまは、このぶんをかいているところです。これからにほんごのふくしゅうをするところです。せんげつこのきょうかしょをかったばかりなので、まだすこししかよんでいません。
a.romaji: Chōdo ima, bangohan o tabeta tokoro desu. Ima wa, kono bun o kaite iru tokoro desu. Kore kara nihongo no fukushū o suru tokoro desu. Sengetsu kono kyōkasho o katta bakari na node, mada sukoshi shika yonde imasen.
a.en: I've just had dinner, this very moment. Right now, I'm writing this sentence. Next, I'm about to review Japanese. I only bought this textbook last month, so I've read just a little of it so far.

items.note: Check: the verb form before ところ matches the moment; たばかり goes with a time that feels recent to you; the predicate is at the end of each sentence.

practice.what: Play in the game's N3 area. Hunt for 〜ところ and 〜ばかり in the dialogues: when you find one, pause and say out loud which moment it is (before, during or right after) and whether the time is clock time (ところ) or felt time (ばかり). Log the session in Immersion → Games, paste one of those lines into 🔬 Anatomy and save it with Mining (⛏), looking up every word you don't know. If you also read an easy manga or a graded reader, hunt there the same way: casual dialogue is full of ところ and ばっかり.

Read one article and listen to its audio. Look for 〜たところ followed by a comma (調べたところ、…): in the news it usually means "when X was done, (it turned out that) Y", not "have just". If none shows up, copy a sentence with 〜ている and say whether it could be swapped for 〜ているところ.

Write 5 sentences of your own: one with るところ, one with ているところ, one with たところ, one with たばかり (something new in your life) and one with るところだった (something that almost happened). Use "Anatomy of what I wrote" and check that the block with ところ／ばかり ended up at the end, with the predicate.
Tap 🔊 on each example in this lesson and repeat along 3 times. Stress the part that changes before ところ (でる・つくって いる・ついた): it is the only thing that changes the moment.
Act out three phone calls and answer each one in 10 seconds or less, with a different moment each time (出るところ / 作っているところ / 着いたところ). Record yourself and listen.

culture.title: Ramen and its rules (slurping is fine)
culture.body: In Japan, **slurping your noodles** (すする) is normal and not rude. That goes for ramen, soba and udon; many people say it cools the noodles down and brings out the aroma. In many ramen shops (ラーメン屋), you buy a **ticket** from a machine at the entrance (券売機, けんばいき) and hand it over at the counter before you sit down. Ramen is usually eaten as soon as it arrives, because the noodles go soft if they sit in the broth (のびる). In small shops with a line outside, the custom is not to linger chatting after you finish, so the seat frees up. In Hakata-style shops you can usually order **替え玉** (かえだま), an extra serving of just noodles for the broth you have left.
culture.try: Next time you eat noodles, quietly narrate each moment in Japanese: 今から食べるところ → 今、食べているところ → 今、食べたところ. And practice ordering extra noodles: 替え玉、お願いします。

checklist: I can say the three moments of an action with ところ without looking: 食べるところ / 食べているところ / 食べたところ.
I can explain why I can't talk right now with 〜ているところだから…
I use 〜たばかり for something recent from my point of view, even days or months ago (先月来たばかり).
I can build "newly X" with 〜たばかりの + noun (買ったばかりの靴).
I know when only ばかり works (a long stretch of time, before a noun) and when only ところ works (before starting or in the middle of the action).
I recognize 〜るところだった (almost…) and the 〜たところ、 of news reports.
I did the homework, checked it against the answer key and redid what I got wrong.
